steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Atlanta GA. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $96,500. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 3 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $670 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 720 sq ft. Deductions: $3,200 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Summary answer (short): You should report the photography income on Schedule C (self‑employment). Your home office is eligible; the actual method (pro rata share of rent) will almost certainly give a bigger deduction than the simplified method. Your $1,500 charitable gift is an itemized deduction but is far smaller than the standard deduction, so you will almost likely take the standard deduction (unless you have lots of other deductible items you didn’t list). The student‑loan interest deduction is limited (maximum $2,500) and phases out at higher incomes — based on your income you may be ineligible to claim the student‑loan interest. You will also owe self‑employment tax on your net photography income and must file the associated forms listed below.

Details, calculations, and required forms

1) Income to report
- W‑2 wages: $96,500 (report on Form 1040).  
- Interest from bank and brokerage: $2,100 + $670 = $2,770 (taxable interest — report on Form 1040; because total interest > $1,500 you’ll also use Schedule B). Expect 1099‑INT or 1099‑B details from those institutions.  
- Photography (self‑employment) income: $16,300 — report on Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business). Even if you didn’t receive 1099s, you must report the income.

2) Business deductions (photography)
- Your “unreimbursed expenses” ($1,050) are deductible only if they are business expenses connected to the photography work. If so, list them on Schedule C (supplies, equipment, advertising, travel, software, etc.). If they were unreimbursed employee expenses (from an employer job), they are NOT deductible under current law (2018–2025).
- Home office: you have a legitimate business use (120 sq ft exclusive use, home = 720 sq ft). Two options:
  a) Simplified method: $5 × square footage = $5 × 120 = $600 deduction.
  b) Actual method: prorate actual home expenses by business percentage. Business percentage = 120/720 = 16.6667%. From rent alone: $1,750 × 12 = $21,000 annual rent × 16.6667% = $3,500. (Plus you can allocate utilities, renter’s insurance, repairs, etc. proportionally if you use actual method.) The actual method here (just using rent) gives $3,500 vs $600 with simplified — so actual will almost certainly be better.
- Note: the home office deduction is taken on Schedule C (Form 8829 if you use the actual method). The deductible amount cannot exceed your net business income (losses may limit the deduction or create carryover rules).

3) Self‑employment tax and related adjustments
- You will owe self‑employment (SE) tax on your net self‑employment income (Schedule SE). Rough estimate if photography net = (16,300 − 1,050 business expenses − 3,500 home office) = 11,750 net:
  - SE tax ≈ 15.3% × 92.35% × 11,750 ≈ $1,660 (Schedule SE).  
  - Half of that SE tax (~$830) is an “above‑the‑line” deduction (adjustment) on Schedule 1 to reduce AGI.
- That reduces taxable income and potentially reduces income tax liability.

4) Student‑loan interest
- The student‑loan interest deduction is an adjustment to income (reported on Schedule 1). Maximum deduction is $2,500 in the year (you cannot deduct $3,200 in full; only up to $2,500). It is subject to income phaseouts based on your modified adjusted gross income (MAGI).
- For recent years the phaseout for single filers started at roughly $75k MAGI and the deduction was eliminated above roughly $90k — thresholds are indexed each year. Given your rough gross income (W‑2 + interest + photography before business deductions = about $115k) you are likely over the phaseout and may not be eligible to take the student‑loan interest deduction. You should check your exact MAGI calculation or ask me to estimate it precisely with any missing data (other deductions, pre‑tax retirement contributions, etc.). Also you’ll need Form 1098‑E from Nelnet showing interest paid to support any claim.

5) Itemize vs standard deduction
- From items you listed, your only itemizable amount is the $1,500 charitable gift. That is far below the standard deduction for single filers, so you will almost certainly take the standard deduction. (Standard deduction for single filers in recent years has been well over $10k; for 2024 it is even higher — you can check the IRS table or I can look up the precise 2024 amount if you’d like.)
- Itemize only if total deductible items (charitable gifts + state and local taxes paid, mortgage interest, medical expenses above threshold, etc.) exceed the standard deduction.

6) Required IRS forms you will likely need
- Form 1040 — main return.
- Schedule 1 (Form 1040) — adjustments to income (half of self‑employment tax, possible student‑loan interest deduction if allowed).
- Schedule C — to report photography business income and expenses.
- Schedule SE — to compute self‑employment tax.
- Form 8829 — Expenses for Business Use of Your Home (if you choose the actual home‑office method).
- Schedule B — for interest and ordinary dividends (required when interest > $1,500).
- Schedule A — only if you itemize (likely you will not here).
- Form 1098‑E (from Nelnet) — lender statement for student loan interest (used to support claim).
- State return — Georgia Form 500 (or appropriate GA return) since you are a Georgia resident.
- Keep 1099s, 1098s, bank/broker statements, and receipts for business/home‑office expenses.

7) Other practical notes and recommendations
- If the $1,050 unreimbursed expenses are business related (e.g., supplies, travel for photography), include them on Schedule C. If they are employee unreimbursed expenses from a W‑2 job, they are not deductible.
- Keep receipts and documentation for the home office (floor plan, square footage calculations, receipts for rent/utility bills) and all business receipts in case of audit.
- Because you have self‑employment income, you should check whether you need to make quarterly estimated tax payments for 2024 (Form 1040‑ES) to avoid underpayment penalties. Your W‑2 withholding may cover some or all tax, but likely you’ll owe some additional tax for the SE tax and extra income taxes.
- If you want to maximize tax benefit for the home office, use actual method (Form 8829) if you have rent and utility amounts to allocate — it usually gives a bigger deduction here.
- Given your likely AGI, you are probably unable to take the full student‑loan interest deduction; confirm with exact MAGI calculation.

8) Quick approximate tax-impact example (estimates)
- Rent home‑office actual deduction (rent only): $3,500.  
- Business expenses total if business‑related: $1,050 + 3,500 = $4,550.  
- Net photography income ≈ $11,750. Self‑employment tax ≈ $1,660 (half deductible ≈ $830).  
- Total taxable income roughly = 96,500 (W‑2) + 11,750 (net biz) + 2,770 (interest) − 830 (half SE) − standard deduction ≈ (this is just an illustration; I can run precise numbers if you want).

Would you like me to:
- Run a more exact estimate of taxable income and tax owed using the precise 2024 standard deduction and MAGI calculations? If so, tell me whether the $1,050 are business expenses and whether you have any other deductions (state taxes paid, mortgage interest, other charitable gifts, retirement contributions), and confirm whether you received a Form 1098‑E for the student loan interest.
- Or draft a checklist/email to your tax preparer with the items and forms to bring?

I’m not a CPA — for complicated issues (student‑loan interest phaseouts, home‑office carryovers if your business has loss, or state‑specific issues) consider confirming with a tax professional.
